explanations.explanation: Romans 9:30 says it plainly: the Gentiles, the people who aren't Israelites, "…did not pursue righteousness…" and still "…have obtained it…" That sounds backward, like winning a race you never signed up for. But the verse says it, and it adds what kind of righteousness it is: one that is by faith. Hold onto that last part, because the whole passage leans on it.

The verse says the opposite. The Gentiles, the people who aren't Israelites, did not pursue righteousness, and they obtained it anyway, a righteousness that is by faith (Romans 9:30). I know that sounds backward. It's like walking into my bakery and finding a full tray cooling that I never mixed. Read the verse again and you'll see it right there.

That's the phrase Paul uses in Romans 9:30: "…a righteousness that is by faith…" Notice what the Gentiles didn't bring to the table. The verse says they did not pursue righteousness, so faith is the only word it gives for how they got it.

Birth never comes up in this verse. Romans 9:30 says the Gentiles obtained "…a righteousness that is by faith…" It's a fair guess, because plenty of us figure family connections must count for something. It's like expecting a free cookie because your cousin works at the bakery. The cashier does not care.

Sacrifice isn't the word in this verse. Romans 9:30 says the Gentiles obtained "…a righteousness that is by faith…" Sacrifice is a big idea elsewhere in the Bible, so I get why it came to mind. But here the verse names faith, and that's what the passage keeps building on.

Romans 9:31 says the opposite: Israel pursued a law of righteousness and "…has not attained it." That's the sting of the verse. They were chasing, and the thing got away from them. So the passage isn't saying they didn't try. It's saying they didn't reach it.

Right, Israel "…has not attained it." (Romans 9:31). Israel pursued a law of righteousness, so the effort was there. It's like me chasing the last cookie crumb across the counter with my mustache and still coming up empty. The verse sets up the next question, which is why.

explanations.answer: They pursued it as if by works
explanations.explanation: That's Paul's answer in Romans 9:32: "Because their pursuit was not by faith, but as if it were by works." The pursuit was there, but it wasn't by faith. Notice the words "as if." Paul says it was as if it were by works.

explanations.answer: They pursued it without the law
explanations.explanation: The text says the opposite. Israel "…pursued a law of righteousness…" (Romans 9:31), so the law was right there in their pursuit. The problem Paul names in 9:32 is that their pursuit "…was not by faith, but as if it were by works." The law wasn't missing. Faith was.

Giving up isn't what the text says. Romans 9:31 says Israel "…pursued a law of righteousness…" so they were pursuing it. Paul gives the reason in 9:32: their pursuit "…was not by faith, but as if it were by works." Quitting isn't the reason he names.

explanations.answer: They will never be put to shame
explanations.explanation: Paul quotes Isaiah, a prophet, and the quote ends: “…the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame.” (Romans 9:33) The stone makes some people stumble, but the one who believes in Him never gets put to shame. That's a promise worth keeping close. It shows up again in Romans 10:11.

The quote doesn't say that. It says “…the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame.” (Romans 9:33) Stumbling and shame are two different things, and the verse only makes the promise about shame. I won't promise a baker a trip-free life. I trip over my own apron strings all the time.

Ruling isn't in the quote. Zion is only where the stone is laid, and the promise is that “…the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame.” (Romans 9:33) It's easy to hear "Zion" and think crowns. The verse keeps it simpler than that.

Paul says, "…my heart’s desire and prayer to God for the Israelites is for their salvation." (Romans 10:1) He addresses them as brothers, and then he opens up. That's not a lecture, it's a prayer. I think you can hear how much he means it.

Prosperity isn't what Paul prays for. Romans 10:1 says his heart's desire and prayer to God for the Israelites is "…for their salvation." I know prosperity sounds nice. But Paul puts his whole heart into one thing, and it's salvation.

Victory isn't the word. In Romans 10:1 Paul says his heart's desire and prayer to God for the Israelites is "…for their salvation." Victory sounds big enough to stamp on a trophy cookie, but the one thing Paul names is salvation. I'd have reached for the big word too.

Romans 10:2 says they are zealous for God, "…but not on the basis of knowledge." So Paul gives them credit for the zeal, then says what was missing. It's like sprinting to a meeting with total passion and no idea which building it's in.

Right, Paul says they're zealous for God, "…but not on the basis of knowledge." (Romans 10:2) He vouches for their zeal first. Then he says it didn't rest on knowledge. Both parts are in the same verse.

Paul says they "…did not submit to God’s righteousness." (Romans 10:3) They were ignorant of it and sought to establish their own. Submitting means going along with God's way instead of building your own. I once decided to stamp a whole batch my way instead of the way that works. The cookies came out as blobs.

Praying isn't what Romans 10:3 says. Paul says they were ignorant of God's righteousness, sought to establish their own, and "…did not submit to God’s righteousness." Prayer shows up in verse 1, but that's Paul praying for them. The thing they didn't do in verse 3 is submit.

Singing never comes up in the verse. Romans 10:3 says they sought to establish their own righteousness and "…did not submit to God’s righteousness." I'd happily hum along in my bakery all day. But the verse is about submitting, not humming.

Paul writes, "…Christ is the end of the law, to bring righteousness to everyone who believes." (Romans 10:4) Notice the end of that sentence: righteousness for everyone who believes. That's the bridge from Israel's chase to the righteousness that comes by faith. Everything else in the passage hangs on this one verse.

Moses, Israel's leader, does show up in the next verse, but only as the one who writes about righteousness by the law (Romans 10:5). The person in verse 4 is Christ. Paul says "…Christ is the end of the law, to bring righteousness to everyone who believes." It's an easy mix-up, since the law and Moses go together in our heads.

Abraham doesn't show up in these verses. Verse 4 names Christ: "…Christ is the end of the law, to bring righteousness to everyone who believes." (Romans 10:4) I'd keep a name from another chapter on the shelf for now. This verse has its own.

Paul says that asking who will ascend into heaven would be "…to bring Christ down…" (Romans 10:6) The righteousness by faith says not to say it in your heart. Heights and I don't mix anyway. My base is gold, but it's not a rocket.

Fire isn't in this verse. Romans 10:6 says asking who will ascend into heaven would be "…to bring Christ down…" Fire does show up in other Bible stories, so I see why it came to mind. Here, it's Christ.

The law isn't what Paul names. In Romans 10:6 he says asking who will ascend into heaven would be "…to bring Christ down…" The law came up earlier in the passage, so it's an easy one to reach for. This verse is about Christ.

The text says, “The word is near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart…” (Romans 10:8) Nobody has to climb up to heaven or dig down to the Abyss to find it. It's closer than that. Paul calls it "…the word of faith we are proclaiming…"
It's the opposite. Romans 10:8 says, “The word is near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart…” That's the whole point of the two questions before it. Nothing needs to be fetched from far away.

Hidden isn't the word. Romans 10:8 says, “The word is near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart…” The verse puts the word in your mouth and in your heart, and says nothing about it being tucked away. It's like me searching the whole counter for a stamp that's already in my mustache.

Paul says you are saved if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord (Romans 10:9). The mouth is where the confessing happens. Verse 10 repeats it: "…with your mouth you confess and are saved." So the first blank is mouth.

The verse says you "…believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead…" (Romans 10:9) Verse 10 backs it up: "…with your heart you believe and are justified…" So the second blank is heart. The belief is on the inside and the confession is on the outside.
Hands aren't in this verse. Romans 10:9 names the mouth for confessing and the heart for believing. My mustache is my hands, so I take that one personally. Sorry, hands, you didn't make the list.

Feet aren't what Paul names here. Romans 10:9 says you confess with your mouth and believe in your heart. Feet do show up later, in verse 15, but those belong to people bringing good news. Different verse, different job.
Eyes aren't in this verse. In Romans 10:9, Paul names the mouth for confessing and the heart for believing. I can't see my way to putting eyes in either blank. The verse doesn't list them.

The verse says the opposite: "…there is no difference between Jew and Greek…" (Romans 10:12) Greek here means someone who isn't Jewish. Paul gives the reason right away: the same Lord is Lord of all. No separate lines at this counter.
Right, Paul says "…there is no difference between Jew and Greek…" (Romans 10:12) The reason is that the same Lord is Lord of all. One Lord, one counter, same welcome for everybody in line.
Paul says the same Lord "…gives richly to all who call on Him…" (Romans 10:12) Richly isn't a small word. It means the giving isn't thin or stingy. And it goes to all who call on Him.

That's the opposite of what the verse says. Romans 10:12 says the same Lord "…gives richly to all who call on Him…" The giving is rich, and it's for all who call on Him. Sparingly is a word for last-crumb situations, and this verse is not one.

Slowly isn't in the verse. Romans 10:12 says the same Lord "…gives richly to all who call on Him…" Richly describes how much, and the verse says nothing about how fast. Slow is how my oven works on a cold day, not how Paul describes this.

Paul asks, "…how can they hear without someone to preach?" (Romans 10:14) It's a chain, and this link is that someone has to speak. Calling needs believing, believing needs hearing, and hearing needs a preacher. Take out one link and the chain drops.

A scroll isn't what Paul names. Romans 10:14 says, "…how can they hear without someone to preach?" The link is a person speaking so others can hear. Reading is a fine thing, but this verse is about hearing.
A temple isn't in the chain. Paul asks, "…how can they hear without someone to preach?" (Romans 10:14) The link he names is a person. He points to someone to preach, not to a place.

Paul asks, "…how can they preach unless they are sent?" (Romans 10:15) Preaching has a sender behind it. Then he quotes Isaiah, a prophet, about the beautiful feet of those who bring good news. That's the next link in the chain, and it's a good one.

Trained isn't the word Paul uses. Romans 10:15 says, "…how can they preach unless they are sent?" Training sounds sensible, and I did train for years to hold a cookie box with my mustache. But Paul's link is being sent.

Welcomed doesn't fit here. The verse says, "…how can they preach unless they are sent?" (Romans 10:15) Welcoming comes up in the next verse, but there it's about the people who heard the good news. Here the preacher is the one being sent.

Paul says, "…not all of them welcomed the good news." (Romans 10:16) So saying everyone welcomed it doesn't match the verse. Then he brings in Isaiah, a prophet, who says, “Lord, who has believed our message?” The text is plain that not everyone welcomed it.

Right, Paul says, "…not all of them welcomed the good news." (Romans 10:16) He backs it up with Isaiah, a prophet, who asks, “Lord, who has believed our message?” The claim in the verse is that not all of them welcomed it.

explanations.answer: By hearing the word of Christ
explanations.explanation: Paul sums it up: “…faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ.” (Romans 10:17) That's where the chain he's been building lands. Faith comes by hearing, and the hearing is by the word of Christ. It's why the preaching mattered so much.
Signs aren't what Paul says. Romans 10:17 says, “…faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ.” Seeing something flashy might sound more exciting. Paul keeps it at hearing.

explanations.answer: By keeping the law of Moses
explanations.explanation: Keeping the law isn't how Paul says faith comes. He says, “…faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ.” (Romans 10:17) Earlier in the passage he said Israel pursued righteousness as if by works. This verse points to hearing instead.

Paul says Isaiah, a prophet, boldly says, “I was found by those who did not seek Me; I revealed Myself to those who did not ask for Me.” (Romans 10:20) So the answer is yes, found by those who did not seek. Paul calls it bold, and I'd say the word fits.

The text says it right there. Isaiah, a prophet, boldly says, “I was found by those who did not seek Me; I revealed Myself to those who did not ask for Me.” (Romans 10:20) Both lines point the same way: found by those who did not seek, revealed to those who did not ask. Paul even calls it bold.

explanations.answer: Holding out His hands to them
explanations.explanation: The line says, “All day long I have held out My hands to a disobedient and obstinate people.” (Romans 10:21) Hands held out, and all day long. I think that picture is hard to forget. Paul says it's what is said about Israel.

explanations.answer: Turning His face away from them
explanations.explanation: That's not what the line says. Romans 10:21 says, “All day long I have held out My hands to a disobedient and obstinate people.” Hands held out is the opposite of a turned face. The words are right there.

The line says something closer than that. Romans 10:21 says, “All day long I have held out My hands to a disobedient and obstinate people.” Holding out hands isn't watching from a distance. It's reaching toward someone.
